Hi everyone, Continuing down the path now with PAZs From the markepedia: PAZ P: The PAZ article is about getting an idea of where price is going to go so you will be able to pick a trade direction with a higher probability of success.

W: By practicing and doing your PAZ homework you will be able to identify the direction of price with a much higher success rate. Once you are able to identify the direction you can then focus on the best My current understanding of PAZs: - Essentially, from my understanding,PAZ is simply the space between FLs.

- To use this for our trading, we should just remember that when price enters a new PAZ from one side, price would then want to continue to go to the other side of the new PAZ. - To enter a new PAZ, price need to engulf the previous PAZ's FL. In RTM, we are taught that after price engulfs into a new PAZ without hitting the other side of the new PAZ, we can enter on the retrace to the FL that caused the engulf (many call this the DP/Decision Point, which, from what I understand, is also a FL).

- Since PAZs are defined as the space between FLs, then naturally there would be PAZ between PCP MPL and base of CP MPL, between two ends of a pole (LQ gap or wide range bars), and between the top and bottom of flags. The best trades should be taken at the edges of these PAZs, i.e.not inside a PAZ. - With the above logic, then we should be able to classify the regions on the chart as either a FL or a PAZ. - PAZs, like price movement, are fractal in nature as well. What looks like a single PAZ in one timeframe can have many FLs and smaller PAZs inside of it. The choice on how we should define our PAZs is ours to make according to which timeframe/scale we want to trade. - This part is if I didn't misunderstood bro Staurum and bro Enkim: Something that I learned from bro Staurum is that we should always look at the higher scale picture for any possible sign of FO that could happen to the lower scale price movement. Here is the post that hinted on this issue. The clue is to look at the HTF picture. Always make sure that the price movement in the HTF has already cleared the MPL of that HTF FL before trying to trade LTF FLs because if the HTF MPL hasn't been hit, price could fake past all of the LTF FLs and go for the HTF MPL, even if there was a valid engulf to the next PAZ edge. Bro Enkim wrote a note (here) that I understood only a few days ago. Thank you bro Staurum and bro Enkim - If price directly hits the other edge of a PAZ, then all trades are off until there is another engulf into another PAZ or if there is a LTF PA telling us to stay within the PAZ (this case, I believe is what we call flagging).

From the markepedia: Engulf: P: "There is no Price Action without an Engulf" and it is what defines our trading. It is our leading "indicator" regarding price intentions. W: Forget about candle engulfs/engulfing patterns. What we look for is Flag Limit Engulfs. Through homework and experience you will learn which FL engulfs are real PA. Once a FL is engulfed price will want to go to the next, but we always have to be mindful of how much it can retrace.

My current understanding of Engulfs: - Real engulfs or PAs are defined as the consumption of all orders inside FLs, i.e. Engulfs arenot simply breaks of local SR, highs and lows, FTRs which are not FLs, or random supply demand zones. I always try to keep this one simple:If I can't find the FL that I think a price movement engulfs, just find the next clear FLs to see the engulf from and scratch the previous mentioned engulf interpretation.

- I always try to remember to draw FLs properly first before assessing engulfs from them. The markepedia gave us a hint on this:Through homework and experience you will learn which FL engulfs are real PA. What looks like a PA/engulf, could be a reaction off the real FL or true supply/demand which is obscured inside a large candle in the tick chart. Please see the following example for a real chart example: - The only useful engulf is the one that hasn't reached its target. We should only look for these types of engulfs. Engulfs that has reached its target is non-tradeable - About this part in the markepedia:Once a FL is engulfed price will want to go to the next, but we always have to be mindful of how much it can retrace, through screen time, I concluded that this has to do with the HTF FL that we want to trade from. The important question to ask about an engulf is:Did the engulf came from the last clean sets of orders, i.e. from the MPL? I would be very careful of trying to trade from a FL if previous price movement didn't clear the HTF FL MPL first beforehand, since a DM of the HTF price action could form after an engulf of a LTF FL if the ITs decide to clear all the orders in the HTF FL. This was my first question in thispostand the answer to that question is summed up in the previous sentences. In short:Always be mindful of the HTF picture, particularly their MPLs - A personal recipe of master Salivan's engulf, which can be read from the FOF Articlestates that the ITs can show their intention by engulfing LTF FL, while at the same time, not engulfing the HTF FL. Personally, for a noob trader such as myself, I believe it is best to leave this advanced master class concept for when we understand all other RTM puzzle pieces. I have not proven this concept myself, but I believe it is safer to wait for whole FL engulfs because there might be clean orders inside an even lower chart than the 1 minute chart, e.g. 10-second or tick charts, above or below the given 1-minute FL.

- An important article from master Salivan is theEngulf/Retrace Article. The conclusion that, I think, we should understand from this article is that: an engulf which didn't reach its' target, would surely have left a set or more clean orders from the FL it came from. It is the retrace to this price level with clean orders (FOF) that we should trade from.

- Also from the engulf/retrace article, the depth of retrace after an engulf depends on whether the target is an important FL or not (i.e. FTR).

Important FLs, from my studies, would have FOs in the form of QM levels that hasn't been touched. Master Mertch's charts show what these FOs look like. If the target is a FL with QM levels that are still clean, then a deeper retrace should be expected as these are ITs' price targets and they would want to get their last orders from the other side of the market to be closed in the FL with clean orders mentioned previously.

- A DM should be expected if FO level doesn't quite touch the MPL of the FL price is reacting to. A DM is essentially, Imho, a FO of a FO level.

- Targets and origins naturally has a double role. They both are one of the same thing. A long origin/source's target is a short origin/source and a short origin/source's target is a long origin/source. These are essentially LS kink / QM levels inside FLs.

- We should check LTF for each QM levels inside the FL we are interested in if we are entering our positions as they may be spiked on the way away from the FL. Do not trade the second and subsequent touches to a QM level if we do not have engulf away from the particular QM level. 1st time back has the most chance of a bounce.

Anxiety, on the other hand, is self-limiting and keeps us immobile. Anxiety paralyzes the mind and hence, the body. This creates invisible boundaries on our capabilities and clouds our judgement. Most of our decisions that comes from anxiety would not be the best ones because we are thinking from an unresourceful state of mind. Anxiety, I believe, comes from irrational worry from going outside our own personal comfort zones.

The solution to anxiety is, in my opinion, acceptance of self and forgiveness of self in situations where mistakes were made. Look at mistakes objectively, then learn from them without emotionally charging the event. Most of the time, when we look back on our past experiences, we are blowing the worry out of proportion and when we actually do what we are supposed to do, nothing as bad or catastrophic as the scenario in our minds occurs.

Intentional immediate action is also a solution that works for me. I find that the longer I wait and think to do something that I worry about, more negativity comes into the mind.

Risk Management & Correlation Considerations Risk management is one thing that I rarely read about in RTM. Probably because this topic seems like a common sense for everybody, but I would like to hear your opinion on this as well since it doesn’t seem like a common sense to me. I apologize in advance if this topic is too basic to post as I want to understand all aspects of trading, not just the technical side of things.

To start, I have understood this one thing that everyone should do:we should never risk everything on a single trade. I understand that we should have many bullets, i.e. capital, to spread the risk for all of our trades, unless we are the IT themselves, which would know where price is going to be next.

Throughout my studies of the markets, there are many money management systems/methods that I have learned, but three in particular stood out. But they each have their own weaknesses as well. These three methods are: 1. Fixed dollar risk 2. Fixed percentage risk 3. Fixed lot size with a defined number of pips for stop loss Fixed Dollar Risk Method If we are using this method, we would set from the beginning a maximum fixed amount of dollars for each trade and we would adjust our lot size according to the fixed dollar amount that we have set at the beginning.

For example, if we have a $10.000 account, we could set that we want to risk $100 maximum on each trade. Given that we would be getting a margin call from our broker when our account equity reaches $2.000, we would need to lose 80 times in a row before getting one. The important part here is that the dollar amount doesn’t change for each successive trade.

To calculate the lot size, we would use the formula below: Lot size= ($ Amount Risk Maximum)/(Lot pip x Amount of pip risk)

For example, for a 100 pip risk on EUR/USD where the lot pip is 10 and $100 maximum risk, we would obtain 0.1 lots as our lot size. By using this lot size, we would ensure that the $100 maximum risk for the trade is fulfilled.

The strength of this fixed dollar risk method is we would know in advance the dollar risk we are risking for each trade, considering there are no gaps or slippage. In the above example, we would know that if we lost 80 consecutive trades, then we would be down to $2.000. If this seems like a small or large dollar amount than expected, we could easily adjust the maximum dollar amount that we would be risking. Increasing the maximum dollar risk would leave us with smaller number of consecutive losses buffer until margin call, and the opposite is also logical.

The weakness for this method is we would have fewer consecutive loss buffers than using the fixed percentage risk, which would have more consecutive losses buffer since the top part of the equation is always changing depending on the account balance.

Fixed Percentage Risk Method If we are using this method, we would set a fixed percentage of the account balance that we would risk for each trade. The lot size would also naturally adjust to the dollars being risked.

To calculate the lot size using this method, we would use the formula below: Lot size= (Percentage risk in decimal x $ Account balance)/(Lot pip x Amount of pip risk)

For example, for a 100 pip risk on EUR/USD where the lot pip is 10 and 1% maximum risk on a $10.000 account, we would also obtain 0.1 lots as our lot size. By using this lot size, we would ensure that the 1% maximum risk for the trade is fulfilled.

If we took a loss on the previous trade, then our account balance would be $9.900. The next trade we take would have $99 as the top part of the equation. Taking the same trade with the same risk parameter as above would obtain 0.09 lots (rounded down).

The strength of this method is that we would automatically lower our risk the more losses we get. We would have a larger number of consecutive losses buffer. Also the size of our wins get larger the more wins we get.

The weakness of this method comes when we have multiple positions across many different markets at the same time. It would be a hassle to re- calculate the lot sizes for all other pairs (assuming they are still pending orders) each time a loss on one trade occurs. The orders that are still open would have a relatively “higher” risk since the account balance would have changed by the time the loss occurred. So while this method has its big strength, it seems impractical from the strategy execution point of view.

Another weakness also comes from the fact that we are using smaller lot sizes each time losses occur. The size of our wins would decrease significantly if we are relatively deep in drawdown (We shouldn't worry about this though if we understand RTM materials properly)

Fixed Lot Size with a Defined Number of Pips for Stop Loss Method If we are using this method, we would set a definite number of lots and a defined number of pips for stop loss. For example we could set to trade 0.1 lots and define the stop loss at 10 pips from our entry. The potential trades that don’t fit into the 10 pip stop loss parameter is automatically discarded.

The strength of this method is we wouldn’t need to calculate the lot sizes and the stop loss pips each time we would want to enter a trade. If a potential trade fits the criteria, we enter the trade. If not, we pass. Decision making would be efficient if we are using this method.

The weakness of this method comes from the changing value of the lot pip for non-base pairs. For example, the lot pip for AUD/USD would not be exactly 10 if we are using a CAD account, while AUD/CAD would be. Essentially, this would vary our risk from time to time, depending on the value of the lot pip.

What I Personally Use I personally use the fixed percentage method for risk management, but I do not strictly adhere to the percentage risk parameter. What I mean by this is at any given time, whenever I want to open a position, I calculate the lot size depending on the present account balance (not equity).

If a loss or a win occurs, I don’t cancel the other pending orders and re- enter the positions according to the new risk percentage parameters. The percentage risk would not be fixed, but in a relatively safe range around the base percentage risk, which, personally, is 0.5% of account balance per trade. This simplifies my lot size calculations a lot.

Correlation Considerations As an additional risk management method, I also use correlation considerations. I would limit my exposure to any given currency to a maximum of 3 at any given time to avoid overexposure, and hence imho, increasing the same type of currency risk.

I would also limit the number of correlated markets to a maximum to 2 at any given time. Examples of correlated markets are, to my knowledge: Gold and silver, AUD/USD and NZD/USD, USD/CAD and CAD/JPY, EUR/USD and USD/CHF, one stock index with another stock index, and many more that I haven't listed here. The concept behind this is also not to increase the same type of currency risks or cancel trades out due to strong negative correlations.

I don’t have experience with this concept, though, and would appreciate any comments or guidance regarding this topic. Hi all, An FL is created when an important barrier is broken. This so-called important barrier can be any of the following: opposing FL, important SR, PCP, end of CP, and QM level.

When it comes to classifying the scale of an FL, we really only need to use two criteria: 1) It's accomplishment - what time scale does the broken barrier belong to?

2) It's visibility - On what time scale is the FL visible?

Now, I see many people still get confused on the issue of scale. When we call something an H4 FL, what do we mean by that, what is an H4 FL? I have not yet come across a definitely guideline on this. Some people call it an H4 FL because it is visible on H4 time frame, but I have recently ask Master IF about this, and he seemed to imply that it's not about visibility, it's more about its accomplishment: So let's say we have a clear swing high/low on H4 being broken/engulfed by a long extended candle (a pole) on H4 timeframe, so we are not going to see a kink on that long candle, but we will find a kink on 1-min chart that coincide with the swing high/low, so this kink visible only on 1-min chart, is actually a H4 kink. And if you can recall, IF has said it several times that we absolutely must go down to the lowest possible timeframe to find our kink.

However, a subsequent post by Master IF confused me Because he seemed to imply in the above post that visibility is what we should use to classify the scale of an FL.

My current understanding on SD zones and Caps on Price: - Price swings from balance to imbalance and back to balance of buyers and sellers repeatedly.

- The rallies and the drops are where the imbalance occurs. A rally is an imbalance on the buy side and a drop is an imbalance on the sell side. - The base is where the balance of transactions between buyers and sellers occur. - The base looks like a square or box. Price finds equilibrium inside the base. The amount of sell vs. buy orders are mostly evenly matched. - The zone between the bottom limit and the top limit of the base is what we call a flag. - SD Zones are decisions whether price is too cheap or too expensive.

- Not all SD zones are created equal, i.e. most are reactions to important DBR/RBD we call Flag Limits.

- RBR and DBD is, in essence, can be reduced to LTF RBDs or DBRs. In my opinion, it is safe to assume that we will not need to concern ourselves with these two things. - Inside a given HTF SD zone, there are many smaller SD zones that can be drawn. This is due to the fractal nature of the markets. Examples inside A and B on the chart.

- When important SD zones (i.e. flag limits) break, we look for the opposite SD zone to be created after their break. This would be the decision that price was not going back inside the base and it is the relevant important one for the next approach.

- Ignored SD zones most of the time would be important when price is coming back from the other side.

- From my studies, I believe the important caps on price held price up or down at least once. The break of such caps on price will create an important caps on price on the reverse side, which we used to call FTR. - Caps on price are safe to trade if we get CP on approach back to the cap.

It is even better to wait for PA/engulf first though for added layer of safety. - Most SD zones are extensively used to create tricks that would provide liquidity for the ITs and, therefore, unreliable as a basis for trades by itself.

I used to think SR levels were all that I need to start trading properly. Mostly the strategy was the usual rejection-type candlestick forming on SR levels.

Surely this leads to eventual frustration due to inconsistencies in the setup. And the thing I hated most of all, which I remembered clearly, was that the levels need to be estimated, i.e. not exact to the pip rejection would occur every time.

Some days, the rejection candle would print above a support line and some days it would print the candle below the support line.

I'm sure you all have tried this type of trading as well at some point before After coming to RTM and reading many materials in this community, I understood (and saw on the charts to prove it myself) that SR is fake propaganda. And the objective of that propaganda is to create liquidity for the ITs.

Let me copy paste this definition of "liquidity" from investopedia: Liquidity describes the degree to which an asset or security can be quickly bought or sold in the market without affecting the asset's price.

Market liquidity refers to the extent to which a market, such as a country's stock market or a city's real estate market, allows assets to be bought and sold at stable prices. Cash is the most liquid asset, while real estate, fine art and collectibles are all relatively illiquid.

Now when I think about the statement "create liquidity", that, in simple terms, would literally mean "create the opposite orders to trade into as not to move price too much" To create liquidity for a truckload of "sell" positions, we would need a truckload of "buy" positions. The reverse applies.

Also, by now, it is a public secret that the ITs want to be the only sellers or buyers at every particular time and market.

To achieve this maximum greed type of trade, they would need to create price movements that builds up a lot of "stop orders" on price levels they would love to maximize their profits on their positions from.

We know that price changes simply when there are imbalance of orders on the bid or offer side (which was summed up previously on the SD zone and caps HW) Why do the ITs need lots of stops to trade into? Simple: it is because they don't want price to move too much away from their best entry point (hence the need for liquidity at their price levels of interest). If the price level they are going to trade in has only a small pool of stop orders, when they place their large orders, even chunks of it, would immediately cause an imbalance and price would move too much away and eat their potential profits.

In order to achieve their goals, i.e. massive amounts of stop orders at desirable price levels, the easiest trick they could do is line up two or three highs/lows. Retailers will see this as an opportunity to fade the SR level once again and place their stops beyond them, where ITs would be the happiest to take these stops. BSZ trade is one of the setups in RTM to exploit this phenomenon.

My current understanding of compression: - Compression (CP) does two things for the ITs: 1. Swapping out their orders from net long to net short or vice versa for their last trade position at the true supply or demand respectively, which, from what I understand, is the MPL. I believe Master Salivan calls this Free Order Flow (Please correct me if I am wrong about your concept of FOF, brother Salivan).

How the ITs achieve this swapping of orders is by creating a series of HHs and HLs, in the case of CP to supply, or a series of LHs and LLs in the case of CP to demand. Retailers love to use these definitions of a “trend” as a base for their “trading systems”. HHs and HLs would create buy stops above the last highs. What the ITs do is they will push price above the previous high and consume all the buy stops sitting there with their sell positions, which would drop price again due to the absence of bids. ITs are essentially reducing their exposure to their long positions. Retailers would believe that this drop is a “retrace” and place more buy stops above the new high and the cycle repeats until the ITs are satisfied with their now net short position. The same logic applies for downwards-sloping CP to true demand.

2. Clearing out any pockets of supply or demand in the way of their desired net position. As an example, if ITs desire a net short position from the true supply as in the case of upwards-sloping CP, it would make their lives much more easier if they clear out the pockets of demand during the CP process for ease of movement through the CP zone.

What I understand by “clearing out pockets of demand” is to take every last sets of orders in the demand zone, which is also the MPL of the demand zone, on the way up. In a perfectly ideal world, every last sets of opposing orders inside a CP (like MPLs of the demand zones in the previous example) would already be cleared on the way to the true supply or demand. Below is IF’s diagram of a perfect CP which I think we all should always keep in mind.

- At the end of CP, we would often see an LQ spike. I personally see this as an odd-enhancer as it is effectively used to create euphoria (in the case of breakout traders) and misery (in the case of the last SD or SR fader). As a side note for myself, I personally prefer to use the term “Liquidity Gap” instead of LQ since I believe there would be a shortage of either bids or offers in an LQ, but that is just me being foolishly over-technical.

This final LQ push to the true zone would create massive opposite orders for the ITs to add to their positions, e.g. lots more of buy orders for ITs to short into in the case of CP to true supply.

- I have also found that some bases of LQ, if aligned with LS levels, could be a nice place to look for bounces, like the below NOK/SEK example. This is already mentioned by IF in the Lite Video #2, which is the Pre-CP (PCP). The other place to look for bounces in price is the MPL of the CP. The area between the MPL of CP and PCP is a flag and we wouldn’t want to trade inside there, unless we are trading a lower TF.

- CP in the direction of the ITs desired final net position can also be used for providing a push to the true zone, as we can best see it from IF’s example below.

- Another thing we should look out for is a HTF level that runs through CPs. IF said (I think it was from the homework analysis section in Lite Video #1)

that when we have a HTF SR running through the middle CP, we should divide the CP into two distinct CPs on each sides of the HTF kink, i.e. one CP above with its MPL and PCP, and the other CP below with its MPL and PCP. The way I understood this is that the HTF kink from the HTF SR level has the potential to turn price in the middle of the CP.

- Last thing that I can include regarding the concept of CP is that we can look for CP to form after price has hit our zone of interest. The Price Reading Article gave out a clue for this: Reaction In LTF, does price react violently to the first decision point? Does it quickly engulf the nearest S/D? (good sign). Does price simply CP away? Maybe it wants to go to the next decision point.

If the reaction from our zone of interest is a CP instead of a liquidity spike in our intended direction of trade, the trade could potentially be in trouble.

Movements above or below the MPL, for demand or supply FLs respectively, are only tricks to build up liquidity for the ITs' massive buy or sell orders respectively.

- With the above logic, it makes the most sense for us to enter only at MPLs for the highest probability trades. Remember that nothing works 100% of the time. What I have found and learned about CPs are as follows: - Upward-sloping CP to a supply zone = price more likely to go down from the supply zone (provided the last demand in CP PAZ is engulfed down)

- Downward-sloping CP from a supply zone = price more likely to go up through the supply zone (provided there is an engulf up of the last supply in CP PAZ and the last demand after CP holds price up)

- Downward-sloping CP to a demand zone = price more likely to go up from the demand zone (provided the last supply in CP PAZ is engulfed up)

- Upward-sloping CP from a demand zone = price more likely to go down through the demand zone (provided there is an engulf down of the last demand in CP PAZ and the last supply after CP holds price down)

- CP followed by LQ without engulf of the approach flag = potential bounce later on from base of LQ - CP that didn't activate immediately, i.e. price didn't engulf the last approach flag in the CP, will still be effective at a later date - The best way to trade a CP is to let price engulf the last approach flag, i.e. the last demand or supply in the CP PAZ, and enter on a RT to a previous DP - If price engulfs the last approach flag in the CP PAZ, then price will slide through to the base of CP PAZ - CP can be used by ITs to push price in the direction of a DP if there is not enough order to reach the DP (easier to explain with a charthere)

- CP away from a demand or a supply level can be used later on to create LQ spikes that could trap retail traders into selling or buying into a demand or supply level, respectively, for the ITs to fill in opposite orders (seehere for example)

Below a LS, there are trapped sellers, maybe primarily from breakout strategies (I've traded one myself called the Ross Hook). When price rises above H to make HH, these trapped sellers want to get out with as minimal loss as possible, so they sell as close to the initial L (which is the LS) to minimize losses.

This closing of sell orders from the previous break of low of LS comes in near the LS for an obvious reason, i.e. to get as close to breakeven as possible, but since every trapped sellers are doing the same thing, there are naturally some buy orders that are left unfilled. This is because to close a sell order, we need buy orders and the buy orders, in this case, is injected to the market at almost the same price are, which is the LS price level or somewhere close to it. There simply aren't many sell orders around that price area to fill all those incoming buy orders. This created the LS kink, which can be seen as a demand zone in the LTFs.

These unfilled buy orders, assuming the ITs' target, i.e. the next important FTR, hasn't been reached, we can safely assume that the ITs will pick up these unfilled buy orders and, afterwards, head for their target.
